lesson.title: Which Slice Is Bigger? Comparing and Ordering Fractions

steps.say: Hi friend, it's Ms. Yuanyuan! Last Friday my neighbours in Surrey ordered one big pizza and cut it into eight equal slices. Sam ate three slices and Priya ate five slices. Sam said, 'We ate the same!' Priya said, 'No, I ate more!' Who is right? That's exactly what fractions help us figure out — they let us compare amounts, not just count whole things.

visual.caption: Sam ate three eighths, Priya ate five eighths of the same pizza

steps.say: Before we compare, here's the most important rule about cutting: the pieces have to be equal. When we cut one pizza into eight equal slices, each slice is called one eighth. The bottom number, eight, tells us how many equal pieces the whole was cut into. The top number tells us how many of those pieces we took.

visual.caption: One pizza, eight equal slices — one slice is one eighth

steps.say: Now here is the lovely part. Sam's slices and Priya's slices are exactly the same size, because they came from the same pizza cut the same way. So we don't need to do anything fancy — we just count the pieces! Three pieces is less than five pieces, so three eighths is less than five eighths. Priya was right. When the bottom numbers match, just compare the top numbers.

visual.caption: Same size pieces, so the longer bar wins: three eighths is less than five eighths

steps.say: Let's try ordering three amounts now. Imagine three water bottles at soccer practice, all the same size, marked in eighths. One is two eighths full, one is five eighths full, one is seven eighths full. Because the bottom number is eight every time, I just line up the top numbers: two, five, seven. So from smallest to largest it goes two eighths, then five eighths, then seven eighths.

visual.caption: Counting in eighths from zero to eight: two eighths is far left, seven eighths is far right

steps.say: Here's a handy trick called using benchmarks. Benchmarks are three easy landmarks: zero, one half, and one whole. Look at four eighths — half of eight is four, so four eighths sits exactly at one half. That means anything smaller than four eighths is less than half, and anything bigger is more than half. Landmarks help you compare quickly without counting every single piece.

visual.caption: Four eighths lands exactly halfway between zero and one whole

steps.say: Let's use benchmarks in a slightly harder example. At a picnic in Stanley Park, three juice jugs are the same size and each is marked in sixths. Noah's jug is two sixths full, Ava's is three sixths full, and Maya's is five sixths full. Half of six is three, so Ava's jug is exactly half. Noah has less than half, and Maya has more than half. Already I can tell Maya's jug has the most!

visual.caption: Noah is under half, Maya is over half — both cut into sixths

steps.say: Now let's write the whole order neatly, from least to greatest. Noah two sixths, Ava three sixths, Maya five sixths. Two, three, five — the top numbers are already in order, and the bars show it beautifully. Notice how the bars get longer step by step. That picture is your proof that you ordered them correctly.

visual.caption: Least to greatest — each bar counts how many sixths

steps.say: So remember, friend: if the bottom numbers are the same, the pieces are the same size, so you simply compare the top numbers. And if you ever feel stuck, ask yourself, 'Is this close to zero, close to half, or close to one whole?' You did wonderfully today.

visual.caption: Same denominator, so more pieces means a bigger fraction

lesson.answer: When the bottom numbers are the same, the pieces are the same size — so just compare the top numbers, and use zero, one half, and one whole as your landmarks.

practice.question: Three same-size one litre water bottles are marked in tenths. Liam's is three tenths full, Sofia's is seven tenths full, and Emma's is five tenths full. Put them in order from least to greatest, and say whose bottle is exactly half full.
practice.answer: Three tenths is less than five tenths, which is less than seven tenths — so Liam, then Emma, then Sofia. Emma's bottle is exactly half full, because five tenths equals one half.
